analysis.one_liner: Bans pharmacy benefit managers from paying brokers kickbacks for steering employer drug plans.
analysis.headline: A House committee voted 34-0 to approve a bill barring pharmacy benefit managers from paying brokers and consultants to win or keep employer drug-plan business; it is waiting for a vote by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the federal pension law (ERISA) to make it illegal for a pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) — the company that runs a health plan's prescription drug benefit — to pay anyone for getting a plan's business, or for a role in the bidding, market checks, and evaluations that decide which PBM gets hired. Payments a PBM makes to brokers or consultants would be presumed to be kickbacks unless the PBM can show written proof that the money pays for real services at a fair market price. The rule would apply to plan years starting after the bill becomes law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees in employer health plans, and the employers who sponsor them. Hidden PBM payments to brokers inflate what employers and employees pay for prescriptions; banning those payments is meant to lower plan costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employer health plan members and employers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a PBM service provider from paying any compensation, direct or indirect, for the referral, placement, retention, renewal of, or access to a covered plan's business, or for inclusion or participation in a request for proposal, market check, evaluation, or any other contracting process.

Presumes that any compensation a PBM pays to a broker, consultant, advisor, or related entity is a kickback unless the parties show contemporaneous written documentation that it reflects fair market value for bona fide services actually rendered and is not related to plan referral or contracting.
Sets an economic-substance test: compensation is judged by how the deal actually works, regardless of how the PBM labels it.
Applies to plan years beginning after enactment, so the rule takes effect promptly.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the employee-benefits brokers and consultants who receive payments from them for steering plan business. They would lose a revenue channel and take on documentation and compliance burdens.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBMs and benefits brokers and consultants

drawbacks.text: The burden is shifted onto brokers and consultants: payments from PBMs are presumed illegal unless backed by contemporaneous written documentation of fair-market-value services, which creates compliance costs and litigation risk for legitimate advisors as well as kickback arrangements.

The bill reaches only compensation paid by the PBM service provider to others; it does not directly restrict the manufacturer rebate system in which drug makers pay PBMs for formulary placement, which many critics see as the larger driver of high drug prices.
As of the record provided, the bill has zero cosponsors, which may signal limited momentum beyond its committee approval.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule is aimed at a well-documented channel of inflated employer drug costs: PBMs paying brokers to deliver plan business or buying a role in the bidding process. The compliance burden on honest brokers is real but modest — bona fide services at documented fair market value remain lawful — and the presumption can be rebutted with paperwork. The main honest criticism is scope: this is one slice of the PBM cost problem, not the rebates manufacturers pay, so the savings for plan members may be smaller than the full problem warrants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House committee with a unanimous 34-0 vote, was reported with an amendment on July 2, and was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills eligible for a House floor vote — but the full House has not voted on it, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen introduced the bill in the House on March 12, 2026, and it was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce.
The committee held a markup on May 21, 2026, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 34-0.

The committee reported the amended bill on July 2, 2026, as House Report 119-729, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 634, meaning it is eligible for consideration by the full House but has not yet received one.
The bill has no cosponsors on record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained a change in the law: PBMs and brokers can continue current payment arrangements until the House votes and a law is enacted. Supporters of lower drug costs have a unanimously committee-approved bill but no scheduled floor vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBMs and brokers, pending a floor vote

for.name: Rep. Rick W. Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it through the Education and Workforce Committee as amended.

for.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on May 21, 2026, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 34-0 vote; reported it July 2, 2026.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers and employee-benefits brokers
against.what_they_did: No member of Congress is on record against the bill; the industries that would lose the kickback channel have an interest in keeping it from becoming law.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote, in committee, was unanimous at 34-0, with no partisan opposition; the sponsor is a Republican and no cosponsors are recorded.

industries.note: The bill bars PBMs from paying anyone for winning or keeping an employer plan's business or for a role in the bidding process, and presumes their payments to brokers are kickbacks without documentation. Those payments are a known way employer drug costs get inflated, so the industry's interest here runs against plan members — though the bill regulates PBMs without dislodging them from their gatekeeper role over drug benefits.

Their compensation from PBMs would be presumed to be a kickback unless documented as bona fide services at fair market value, eliminating undisclosed fees tied to steering plan business. Legitimate, documented advisory work remains lawful, so the loss is limited to the hidden-fee channel.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Union Calendar with unanimous committee support but no cosponsors and no scheduled floor vote. A standalone health-billing bill like this most often gets floor time only when attached to a larger package; unless leadership schedules it or folds it into a broader PBM or health-cost bill, it is likely to remain on the calendar when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
